extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy (metaphysics, Schopenhauer studies)
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of Schopenhauerian metaphysics arguing the primacy and indestructibility of the will, the secondary/phenomenal status of knowledge/intellect, and a palingenetic account of rebirth (distinct from simple metempsychosis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of the will over intellect
rubrics_metrics.description: The will is the thing in itself; the intellect/knowledge is only a secondary phenomenon, introduced by animal nature and conditioned by the brain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation: “as soon as I know, I have an idea; but this idea, just because it is my idea, cannot be identical with what is known… therefore for a knowing consciousness there can be always only phenomena.” The intellect is a reflex of the will, dependent on the somatic life and perishing with the brain; the will alone is original and conditions phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indestructibility of the will
rubrics_metrics.description: The will is not subject to temporal determinations (beginning, end, continuance) and therefore remains untouched by death; death destroys only the phenomenal knowing-consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supporting points: empirical birth/death apply only to phenomena; the thing-in-itself (the will) ‘constantly retains that existence to which the conceptions of beginning, end, and continuance are not applicable.’ Thus consciousness perishes but the underlying will endures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fear of death rooted in the will, not knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: The fear of death springs directly from the blind will to live (not from rational knowledge of life's value); if one were merely a knowing being, death would be indifferent or welcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: philosophers prove death no evil on knowledge grounds, yet fear remains because it is rooted in the will. The will’s ‘blindness’ makes clinging to life inevitable despite rational conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge/idea vs will: incommensurable laws
rubrics_metrics.description: The phenomenal world (idea) and the thing-in-itself (will) obey heterogeneous and incommensurable laws; concepts like arising and passing away apply to phenomena but not to the will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: procreation considered from will (immediate sensual pleasure) versus idea (ingenious organism design) shows that the laws governing appearance and underlying reality differ fundamentally; what is meaningful in one domain can be meaningless in the other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procreation as dual phenomenon (will vs idea)
rubrics_metrics.description: Procreation appears internally as the will’s blind, pleasurable impulse, and externally as the idea’s complex, designed organism; this contrast illustrates the fundamental opposition of the two sides of the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expanded: from the will it's ‘an impetuous, blind impulse,’ from the idea it is ‘the most arduous work of profound reflection.’ This opposition underlines the invalidity of phenomenal laws for the will.

rubrics_metrics.name: Palingenesis model of rebirth (distinct from metempsychosis)
rubrics_metrics.description: After death the individual intellect (mortal) perishes but the will (immortal) persists and, under world-processes, assumes a new intellect in a new individual—so rebirth is palingenesis (reappearance with a new intellect), not the survival of the full knowing self.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key points: the new being has no recollection because memory belongs to intellect; the will is the enduring substance and successive births are ‘the succession of the life-dreams of a will’ until it can deny itself. The term palingenesis is preferred to metempsychosis because only the will (not the knowing soul) persists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inheritance: character from father, intellect from mother (as explanatory principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Character (the will) is inherited from the father whereas the intellect is inherited from the mother, which helps explain how the will survives and acquires a new intellect at rebirth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citation: the text refers ahead to chapter 43 for fuller explanation; used to justify how a persisting will can obtain a new intellect ‘received through a new generation’ and thus become a new being without memory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited recognition across births (remembrance as obscure intimation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition of previous lives in subsequent births is generally limited to an obscure reminiscence; distinct recollection is rare (exception: Buddha allegedly remembers earlier births).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References: Jâtaka (Buddha’s recollection) noted as exceptional; ordinary recognition is vague and cannot be brought to distinct consciousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Esoteric Buddhism aligns with palingenesis
rubrics_metrics.description: The esoteric doctrine of Buddhism (as presented in some sources) conforms to the palingenesis view, teaching a morally based reappearance rather than literal metempsychosis as commonly preached to the masses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References: Spence Hardy’s Manual of Buddhism and other works are cited; public/simple metempsychosis is said to be a comprehensible substitute for the masses while the esoteric doctrine is subtler and nearer the author’s view.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demographic/empirical phenomena cited as support for palingenesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical observations—e.g., increased births after high mortality events (Black Death), frequent twin births, and correlated death-birth rates—are presented as indicative of a metaphysical connection between death and birth (one being arising from another).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sources cited: F. Schnurrer (Chronik der Seuchen), Casper (Ueber die wahrscheinliche Lebensdauer des Menschen). Author argues a physical causal connection is impossible, so the pattern suggests a metaphysical ground linking old deaths and new births.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principium individuationis creates illusion of separateness; unity of will
rubrics_metrics.description: Space and time as principium individuationis produce apparent individuation; in the thing-in-itself this distinction between individual and species disappears—both are one will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: what appears as separate individuals in time/space are, in the underlying reality, expressions of the same enduring will; concepts like beginning and end apply only to the phenomenal, individuated level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical and cross-cultural prevalence of metempsychosis belief
rubrics_metrics.description: Belief in metempsychosis (or related doctrines) is widespread across cultures and history (Vedas, Pythagoreans, Egyptians, Greeks’ mysteries, Druids, parts of Islam in India, many indigenous peoples), with Judaism and its derivative religions as notable exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and citations given: Vedas, Plato, Orpheus, Pythagoreans, Edda, Druids, Bohrahs, accounts of Australian natives, references to works by Herodotus, Ungewitter, and others. The claim: metempsychosis is a 'natural conviction' of mankind and widely attested.
